items.prose: A book has 50 loans. A tree is grown on one bootstrap sample of 50 draws.
items.question: What is the chance a given loan is left out of the sample?

widget.label: Chance the loan is left out

feedback.generic: Not quite right. All 50 draws must miss the loan.

byKey.one: $1/50$ is the chance one draw picks it. All 50 draws must miss it.
byKey.in: That is the chance it is drawn at least once.

explain.text: Each draw misses the loan with probability $49/50$, and the draws are independent: $(49/50)^{50} = 0.364$.

items.prose: Each tree in a forest has prediction variance 0.20 for a loan, and any two trees have correlation 0.25. The forest has 200 trees.
items.question: What is the variance of the forest's average prediction?

feedback.correct: The floor, 0.05, is nearly all of it.

byKey.ind: $\sigma^2/B$ assumes independent trees. Add the floor $\rho\sigma^2 = 0.05$.

explain.text: $0.25 \times 0.20 = 0.05$ survives any number of trees; the rest is $0.15/200 = 0.00075$. Only a lower $\rho$ would help much.

items.prose: Five loans, each with the average $P(\text{default})$ from its out-of-bag trees. The forest predicts default above 0.5.
items.question: What is the out-of-bag error?

feedback.correct: Two of five OOB predictions are wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each average into a prediction, then count the wrong ones.

byKey.acc: 0.6 is the OOB accuracy. The error is the share wrong.
byKey.one: Check loan 4 too: 0.6 predicts default, but it repaid.

explain.text: Predictions are 1, 0, 0, 1, 1. Loan 3 defaulted but scored 0.4; loan 4 repaid but scored 0.6. Error $2/5 = 0.4$.

items.prose: A forest's impurity importances put `client_id`, a number unique to each borrower, second of 12. On the test set its permutation importance is −0.002.
items.question: What is the best reading?

options.text: client_id is memorised noise: impurity importance rewards its many thresholds
client_id carries a hidden signal that permutation importance misses
options.why: Permutation importance on new data is the direct test of usefulness; −0.002 is noise around 0.

options.text: The shuffle was unlucky; repeat it until the drop is positive
options.why: Repeating shuffles changes the noise, not the answer. Ten more will still average near 0.

options.text: Borrower identity drives default, so keep it
options.why: An id can stand for real history, but this model gains nothing from it on new borrowers.

feedback.correct: Many distinct values let trees chase noise.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall loan_id: 0.158 impurity, −0.008 on new loans.

explain.text: A unique id offers a threshold between every pair of borrowers, so deep trees use it near their leaves. Held-out permutation importance shows it is worth nothing.

items.prose: You fit `RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)` on 9 features to forecast credit spreads. In scikit-learn 1.6 its default is `max_features=1.0`.
items.question: What have you fitted?

options.text: Bagged regression trees: every split sees all 9 features
A forest with $m = p/3 = 3$, the textbook default
options.why: $p/3$ is the usual recommendation, not scikit-learn's regressor default. Set `max_features=1/3` to get it.
$\sqrt{p}$ is the classifier's default. The regressor's is 1.0, all features.

options.text: Trees that each use one feature
options.why: 1.0 is a fraction of the features, so all 9.

feedback.correct: Check `max_features` before you call it a forest.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `max_features=1.0` is a fraction of the 9 features.

explain.text: A float means a share of the features: 1.0 is all of them, which is bagging. Pass `max_features=1/3` for the $p/3$ rule, or tune it with OOB.

items.prose: A forest predicts whether each week's 4-week forward return is positive, one row per week. Its `oob_score_` is 0.68; a walk-forward test gives 0.51.
items.question: Which number should go in the report?

options.text: 0.51: neighbouring weeks share 3 of 4 return weeks, so OOB votes saw near copies
0.68: OOB is an honest test because no tree saw its own row
options.why: Each row's OOB trees saw its neighbours, which share most of its label.
Averaging an inflated number with an honest one is still inflated.

options.text: Neither: grow more trees until OOB matches walk-forward
options.why: More trees steady the OOB estimate; they do not remove the leak.

feedback.correct: Overlapping labels break the OOB assumption.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what each row's OOB trees know about it.

explain.text: OOB assumes exchangeable rows. With overlapping labels, the neighbours a tree drew are near copies of the OOB row, so the score flatters. Report the walk-forward result.

items.prose: Two features, debt-to-EBITDA and net debt-to-EBITDA, have correlation 0.95. Their permutation importances are 0.006 and 0.004. A colleague drops both as unimportant.
items.question: What should you expect?

options.text: A large fall in accuracy is possible: each was small only because the other covered for it
A fall of about 0.01, the sum of the two importances
options.why: You added the two small numbers. Each was measured with its twin still present.

options.text: No change, since both are unimportant
options.why: Each alone is redundant; together they may carry the leverage information.

options.text: A gain, because redundant features overfit
options.why: Redundancy rarely costs a forest much. Losing both can cost a lot.

feedback.correct: Test a correlated group by dropping it together.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall cover and cover_ttm: 0.029 and 0.015, yet 9.5 points together.

explain.text: Permutation importance of one feature leaves its twin in place, so it understates the pair. Refit without both, an ablation, to see what they carry together.

items.prose: One analyst's forecast error has sd 4.0%. The average of 50 analysts has error sd 2.9%. Assume every pair has the same correlation $\rho$.
items.question: What $\rho$ does that imply?

feedback.correct: The analysts' errors are about half shared.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square the sds, then solve the variance formula for $\rho$.

byKey.ratio: $2.9/4.0$ compares sds. The formula is in variances: square them first.
byKey.sq: $8.41/16$ ignores the $(1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$ term. Include it, then solve.

explain.text: $8.41 = 16\rho + 0.32(1 - \rho)$, so $8.09 = 15.68\rho$ and $\rho = 0.516$. Even 1,000 analysts would leave an sd of about $4\sqrt{0.516} = 2.87\%$.
